adoption.body: Businesses in the Census Bureau's survey report current AI use at 21.8%. Expected use within six months is 25.9%, but the measure records stated intent rather than current use. Near-term expectations therefore remain close to the current-use base.
adoption.headline: Business AI intentions sit just above reported current use

compute.body: Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, with capacity utilization at 81.7%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%, but utilization was lower at 72.2%. Output is rising in both industries, while the utilization gap indicates different pressure on installed capacity.
compute.headline: Compute output is growing under different capacity conditions

data_center.body: Available project records list 3,068 operating sites and 1,556 sites in development, a ratio of 0.51. Separately, 894 sites are tracked in the active pipeline. Meta is reportedly planning a further expansion of its Eagle Mountain campus in Utah, providing a current example of continued campus expansion without establishing the pace of the wider pipeline. These site counts describe the breadth of activity, not the power or compute capacity the projects will deliver.
data_center.headline: Project records show one development site for every two operating sites, with 894 sites tracked as active

finance.body: Operating cash flow is 1.42 times current CapEx, while cash reserves are equivalent to 0.96 years at the current spending pace. Borrower strain is 26.0, while lender strain is -13.5. The funding picture therefore combines cash-flow coverage above current CapEx with reserve coverage below one year and strain readings of opposite signs.
finance.headline: Cash flow covers current CapEx, but reserves alone fall short of a year

grid_storage.body: The active queue contains 2,061 GW, including 552.7 GW of storage, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Earlier experience cautions against reading the full queue as future operating supply: only 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. That historical outcome is not a forecast for the current queue. Pennsylvania regulators are reportedly preparing to consider ratemaking, return on equity and curtailment as data-center load grows, putting pricing and operating rules alongside the physical buildout.
grid_storage.headline: The 2,061-GW grid queue remains mostly outside advanced stages

macro.body: Financial signals are mixed rather than uniformly weak. The AI Equity Index and average sector trading pressure edged lower, yet 61.3% of covered companies remain positive over one year and the median return increased to 14.8%. Operating cash flow equals 1.42 times current CapEx, while cash reserves equal 0.96 years of spending. Borrower strain is 26.0, compared with lender strain of -13.5. The funding picture combines support from current internal cash generation with a sub-one-year reserve cushion and divergent borrower and lender conditions. Physical expansion is visible in current output as well as project records. Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, and semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%. Data-center records show 0.51 development site per operating site, while 894 sites are tracked in the active pipeline. Yet only 24.2% of the 2,061-GW active interconnection queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages, and just 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. The historical rate is not a forecast, but it cautions against treating proposed capacity as delivered supply. Pennsylvania regulators are reportedly considering ratemaking, returns and curtailment as data-center load grows, a reminder that grid expansion also requires decisions about prices and operating rules. Broad deployment remains gradual. Current AI use is reported by 23.2% of businesses, compared with 27.3% expecting use within six months, a 4.1-point gap. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, and the strongest channel is growing 0.8%. Nonfarm-business productivity is growing 2.2%, but that aggregate does not identify an AI contribution. For now, the evidence is clearer on infrastructure activity than on broad labor-market or productivity effects.
macro.headline: Physical buildout continues, but pipeline conversion and broad deployment remain limited

market.body: The AI Equity Index slipped to 32.2 and average sector trading pressure to 50.0. The share of covered companies with positive one-year returns also edged down to 61.3%, but the median one-year return increased to 14.8%. The combination shows softer breadth without a uniform deterioration in company-level performance.
market.headline: Market indicators edge lower, but the median one-year return improves

water.body: Current county drought data cover 1,434 of 1,482 data-center campuses, or 96.8%. The screen identifies 275 campuses in counties where some area is under D2-or-worse drought. This improves geographic exposure context, but county-level screening neither places each campus within the affected area nor measures facility water demand.
water.headline: County drought screening now covers nearly all mapped campuses

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The AI Equity Index edged down to 31.7, but 62.7% of covered companies now have positive one-year returns and the median one-year return rose to 15.5%. Average sector trading pressure increased more materially to 52.2. The latest readings therefore show improving return breadth and trading pressure beneath a slightly lower aggregate index.

headline.text: Return breadth improves even as the AI Equity Index edges lower

body.text: The Chicago Fed NFCI edged higher but remains at -0.56; its three-month change is -0.05. Borrower strain is 26.0, while lender strain is -13.5, leaving the tracked strain measures on opposite sides of zero. Large-project reports are similarly split: Reuters said banks provided a $22 billion chip loan to a Blackstone-Alphabet AI cloud venture, while Oracle's $18 billion data-center debt was under pressure. The Federal Reserve also raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4%, adding a higher policy rate to this mixed backdrop.

headline.text: Broad finance readings remain mixed as large project-debt reports diverge

body.text: Computer and peripheral-equipment output is growing 9.2%, with capacity utilization at 81.7%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output is growing faster, at 11.5%, while utilization is lower at 72.2%. An advanced-packaging park anchored by TSMC has also broken ground in Taiwan. The project marks additional construction in the packaging supply chain, but it does not yet change the current production readings.

headline.text: Compute output grows as a TSMC-anchored packaging park moves into construction

body.text: Available project records list 3,068 operating sites and 1,556 in development, a ratio of 0.51. Separately, 894 sites are tracked in the active pipeline. Recent reports show why those counts should not be read as delivered capacity. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott broadened a moratorium on data-center approvals to include environmental permits, and Oracle reportedly issued a force majeure notice to Blue Owl after setbacks at the Project Jupiter campus. The policy action and project setback are specific cases, but both make conversion risk more concrete.

headline.text: The site pipeline remains large, while recent reports make conversion risk more concrete

body.text: The active interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, including 552.7 GW of storage, but just 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Earlier outcomes remain a warning against treating the full queue as future supply: 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation, though that is not a forecast for current projects. In Texas, regulators reportedly softened data-center interconnection rules, while Microsoft said it was preserving its ability to challenge a decision on transmission costs. The developments keep both connection terms and cost allocation in focus.

headline.text: The grid queue remains mostly outside advanced stages as Texas revisits interconnection rules and costs

body.text: The county screen now places 302 data-center campuses, or 21.1% of campuses with county drought data, in counties where some area is under D2-or-worse drought. A stricter screen places 261 campuses, or 18.2%, in counties where at least one-quarter of the area is under D2-or-worse drought. Both measures increased slightly. These county-level readings identify geographic exposure, not a campus's exact location within the drought area or its water use.

headline.text: A larger share of data-center campuses is located in drought-affected counties

body.text: Businesses reporting current AI use increased slightly to 23.8%, while 27.6% expect to use it within six months. The gap narrowed to 3.8 percentage points, so stated near-term intentions remain close to reported use. The leading sector's current-use reading rose more materially to 49.0%, about twice the overall rate. Aggregate adoption is moving gradually, with much deeper use in at least one sector.

headline.text: Business AI use rises, but the leading sector is already near 50%
AI infrastructure activity continues, while project conversion and business diffusion remain uneven

paragraphs.text: Physical activity remains substantial. Computer and peripheral-equipment output is growing 9.2%, and semiconductor and electronic-component output 11.5%; an advanced-packaging park anchored by TSMC has also broken ground in Taiwan. Available data-center records show 0.51 development site for every operating site, while 894 sites are separately tracked in the active pipeline. A reported $22 billion bank loan for a Blackstone-Alphabet AI cloud venture provides a current example of large-scale financing. These signals describe activity across the supply chain, not the operating capacity that will ultimately be delivered.

Conversion remains the central uncertainty. The active grid interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Just 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation, a historical result rather than a forecast for current projects. Recent developments add more immediate constraints: Texas broadened a moratorium on data-center approvals to include environmental permits even as state regulators softened interconnection rules, and Oracle reportedly issued a force majeure notice after setbacks at Project Jupiter. Approvals, grid terms and project execution can therefore move in different directions even while the pipeline remains large.

Business deployment remains partial and uneven. Current AI use rose to 23.8%, compared with 27.6% expected within six months, leaving a gap of 3.8 percentage points. The leading sector is already at 49.0%, showing much deeper use than the aggregate rate, but only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth. Nonfarm-business productivity is growing 2.2%, though that economywide measure does not identify an AI contribution. For now, the evidence remains clearer on physical activity and project formation than on broad labor-market or economic effects.
